A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FairDICE replication study despite the changed title. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and matchable, including relocated results and renumbered appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original replication experiments, corrected-implementation comparisons, sensitivity studies, and GroupFair and Minecart-RGB evaluations, beyond figures reproduced from prior work.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results throughout Section 4 and the appendices, including benchmark comparisons and experiments on biased data and complex environments.

M1.justification: Both versions already include the broadcasting correction, gradient-penalty variants, log and piecewise-log utilities, and the same architectures and learning procedures. Revised explanations and newly disclosed evaluation details do not establish a change to the method.

E1.justification: The environments, datasets, and negative-reward, biased-data, high-dimensional-reward, and image-observation scenarios are retained. The uniform/narrow/wide preference-distribution experiment in v2 Appendix K was already reported in v1 Section 4.3.2.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain BC(P), MODT(P), MORvS(P), unconditioned BC, utilitarian variants, and the same reference policies. The expanded discussion of prior BC performance does not introduce an additional evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: Section 4.2.2, footnote 10, newly reports a qualitative evaluation comparison using sampled Gaussian actions instead of mean actions. This adds a limited evaluation variant; existing benchmark splits, training budgets, normalization, and metrics remain unchanged. Jain's fairness was already evaluated before its formula was added.

E4.justification: v2 adds a brief sensitivity finding that sampling Gaussian actions reduces performance, and asserts that cosine scheduling and orthogonal initialization are necessary for strong BC performance. These additions lack quantified ablation results. Existing hyperparameter, reward-transformation, imbalance, and scaling analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Seed counts, uncertainty displays, the five-seed selection/five-held-out-seed protocol, and Appendix D's Kruskal-Wallis tests are unchanged. No additional statistical procedure is documented for the new qualitative sensitivity assertions.

E6.justification: Matched numerical tables and plotted results are retained, including v1 Table 1 becoming v2 Table 5. v2 adds the qualitative action-sampling deterioration finding. Appendix H also narrows its empirical summary of typically successful beta values from 0.1 or 1.0 to 0.1.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 corrects the nonlinear target from sum_i mu_i u_i(J_i) to sum_i u_i(J_i), distinguishing it from the weighted linear surrogate. Appendix A's losses and the sign-error argument, moved from Appendix K to L, are unchanged. Section 2.1 also introduces a reversed policy conditional, pi(s|a), inconsistent with Equation 7.

C1.justification: The introduction and discussion replace the claim that hyperparameter tuning necessarily requires online evaluation with the qualification that offline tuning is challenging but possible. The discussion additionally emphasizes strong BC performance as a benchmark concern. The central implementation-error, sensitivity, and scalability claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 expands the explanation of BC success to include reward correlation, similar behavior across preferences, training choices, and averaging noisy actions. It clarifies the positive-expected-return requirement and recommends more challenging benchmarks. These refine the retained interpretation that existing results do not isolate FairDICE's welfare mechanism.

D1.justification: Footnote 10 newly discloses that continuous-policy evaluation uses Gaussian means rather than sampled actions. Cosine scheduling and orthogonal initialization receive more emphasis but were already documented in v1 Appendix C. Architecture specifications, hardware information, training budgets, and code-access references are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Paine et al. on offline hyperparameter selection, Loshchilov and Hutter on scheduling, and Nachum and Dai and Mao et al. for DICE theory. These provide limited additional context and qualify the offline-tuning criticism without substantially changing the study's research positioning.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, selected background and discussion paragraphs are rewritten, and explanatory transitions and footnotes are added. Preference-distribution material moves to Appendix K, shifting the final appendix to L. The overall narrative and section structure remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 3 changes from three panels to a four-panel arrangement, adding a HalfCheetah-amateur view already present in Figure 17. The preference-distribution table moves from the main text to Appendix K, Figure 5 shifts pages, and bibliography and appendix layouts receive localized adjustments.

improvement.justification: v2 improves the precision of the objective and offline-tuning discussion and discloses mean-action evaluation, helping readers interpret and reproduce the retained findings. The gains are limited: new mechanism and sensitivity assertions lack quantified supporting analyses, and Section 2.1 introduces a reversed policy conditional. The empirical evidence otherwise remains substantially unchanged.
